In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

p53 germlines are associated with the development of sarcoma, breast cancer and brain cancer in children, and adrenocortial cancer in both children and adults, and that the presence of any one of these cancers in the family history is sufficient to warrant p53 testing.

p53 mutation testing in patients and families with cancer is a reasonable approach to identifying a high-risk subset of cancer-proned families, and should be performed in patients and families who have a personal or family history consistent with classic LFS or Chompret syndrome.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the p53 mutation prevalence table is a useful tool for clinicians in identifying families with a high risk of p53-related tumors.
p53 mutation carriers are at high risk for sarcoma, brain tumors, and ACC, and that a comprehensive family history is critical to identify families at risk for germline mutations in the p53 gene
the classic Li Fraumen syndrome (LFS), and Chompret (2001) criteria are very useful for identifying a subset (95%) of cancer prone families with p53 gene mutations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the clinical features of p53 mutation carriers are more extensive than those of classic Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
the classic LFS criteria are still useful, but the Chompret criteria are even better at predicting the presence of a p53 mutation.
the classic LFS and the Chompret criteria have a very high positive predictive value (PPV) for identifying families with a p 53 mutation.
